title: The River That Learned to Smile

pages.text: Mr Tweneboah put two pictures on the board. The first showed a brown river full of boats, rubbish and crowded huts on the banks. The second showed a clear river with trees, bridges and people walking beside it. “Same river,” he said. “Taken about thirty years apart. It is the Singapore River.”
sentences: Mr Tweneboah put two pictures on the board.
The first showed a brown river full of boats, rubbish and crowded huts on the banks.
The second showed a clear river with trees, bridges and people walking beside it.
“Same river,” he said.
“Taken about thirty years apart.
It is the Singapore River.”
pages.alt: Two photographs side by side: a dirty, crowded river and the same river clean with a tree-lined walkway.

pages.text: “By the 1960s and 1970s,” said Mr Tweneboah, “the river was an open sewer. Street hawkers, small factories, pig and duck farms, boats unloading cargo and thousands of homes without toilets all drained waste into the river and into the Kallang Basin. People said nothing could live in it.” Samir wrinkled his nose.

People said nothing could live in it.” Samir wrinkled his nose.
pages.alt: A drawing of a crowded riverbank with boats, stalls, farms and houses all draining into the water.

pages.text: “In 1977 the government made a master plan,” said Mr Tweneboah. “The prime minister set a target: clean the river in ten years. The work was declared complete on 2 September 1987. A leading civil servant led the team, and the prime minister promised gold medals to the officers who did the job.” “Ten years,” said Obaa. “It was not magic. It was a deadline.”
sentences: “In 1977 the government made a master plan,” said Mr Tweneboah.
“The prime minister set a target: clean the river in ten years.
The work was declared complete on 2 September 1987.
A leading civil servant led the team, and the prime minister promised gold medals to the officers who did the job.” “Ten years,” said Obaa.
“It was not magic.
It was a deadline.”
pages.alt: A calendar showing 1977 and 1987 joined by a long arrow and a gold medal.

pages.text: “It was not only about the river,” said Mr Tweneboah. “About forty-six thousand people living along the banks were moved. Around five thousand street hawkers were moved to new hawker centres near where they had worked. Hundreds of pig and duck farms were moved out. Sewers were built, drains covered, the riverbed dredged, and floating barriers trapped rubbish.” “So they were not simply thrown out,” said Obaa. “They were given places to go,” said Mr Tweneboah.

Hundreds of pig and duck farms were moved out.
Sewers were built, drains covered, the riverbed dredged, and floating barriers trapped rubbish.” “So they were not simply thrown out,” said Obaa.
“They were given places to go,” said Mr Tweneboah.
pages.alt: People walk from crowded huts into tidy new homes and a new market hall.

pages.text: “The clean-up cost an estimated three hundred million Singapore dollars, not counting the money paid to people who moved,” said Mr Tweneboah. “It was serious money and serious work. The prime minister also wanted people to form new habits, because a clean river can be dirtied again in a week.” “And in a week,” said Samir, “someone can throw a sachet.”

pages.alt: A bag of coins beside a clean river and a sign that reads: new habits.

pages.text: “Now compare our own waters,” said Mr Tweneboah. He put a photograph of a drain on the board. “One article says Accra signed a plan in 2012 to dredge the Odaw and restore the Korle Lagoon, with a price of around six hundred and sixty million US dollars. The writer says the promised change never came. Another report says only about a third of the money for a later flood project had been spent by mid-2025. These are claims to check, not final facts.”

The writer says the promised change never came.
Another report says only about a third of the money for a later flood project had been spent by mid-2025.
These are claims to check, not final facts.”
pages.alt: A photograph of a drain choked with waste beside a map of the Odaw and the Korle Lagoon.

pages.text: “Are we the same as Singapore?” asked Obaa. “No,” said Mr Tweneboah. “It is a small island city with a different history, size and budget, and its government was strong in ways some people dislike. We should not copy it blindly. But we can learn four things: a clear deadline, fair treatment for people who must move, real drains and sewers, and leaders who keep going until it is done.”

We should not copy it blindly.
But we can learn four things: a clear deadline, fair treatment for people who must move, real drains and sewers, and leaders who keep going until it is done.”
pages.alt: A chart with four ticks: deadline, fairness, drains and sewers, persistence.

pages.text: Obaa drew a picture of the Korle Lagoon with fish, trees and a children’s playground on its banks. Under it she wrote: “If a river could be cleaned in ten years, ours can be too. But it will take all of us.” Samir pinned it to the wall. Mr Tweneboah looked at it for a long time. “Then you have started,” he said. The end.

They should stay in the dirty river
